entries.title: Everything You Need to Know for Commanders-Giants
entries.summary: Key matchups, how to watch, pregame reading and more for Week 5.
entries.content:
The Commanders return home Sunday to face the Giants, who are off to a hot start under new coach John Harbaugh. Jayden Daniels is expected to return after a two-week absence, as Washington faces a pivotal Week 5 divisional matchup.

Here’s everything you need to know.

Kickoff: 1 p.m. ET at Northwest Stadium, Landover, Maryland.

TV: Fox

Betting Lines

Lines from DraftKings, as of Friday. 

Spread: Commanders -3.5

Money line: Commanders -192, Giants +160

Over/under: 42.5 points

Pregame Reading

The Commanders’ season is only four games old, but it already feels like it’s on the brink. Dave Sheinin and Martenzie Johnson examined the team at the quarter mark of the season and sorted through the good and the bad.

After a slow start to the season, the Commanders pass rush is starting to thrive. The unit was disruptive in London against the Colts and will need to sustain that success against the Giants. Johnson has more on Washington’s defense.

Daniels will return under center two weeks after he dislocated his elbow for the second time in 10 months. With Marcus Mariota out with an MCL sprain, Daniels’ return quickly became a necessity.

About the Giants

The Giants’ injury report rivals the Commanders’ in its scope. Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart is out for the season with a knee injury, as is defensive end Brian Burns, depriving the Giants of arguably their most important players on both sides of the ball. Earlier this week, wide receiver and return specialist Braxton Berrios was ruled out for the season with a foot injury.

Star wide receiver Malik Nabers missed Wednesday due to knee soreness, but he will play on Sunday. Jameis Winston is expected to start under center, but recently acquired quarterback J.J. McCarthy has drawn rave reviews for his ability to quickly pick up the team’s playbook.

One Big Question

Can the Commanders keep Daniels upright?

The last time Daniels returned from a dislocated elbow, he reinjured it in his first game back and was ruled out for the rest of the season. The Commanders are already without starting left tackle Laremy Tunsil, and rookie Athan Kaliakmanis is Daniels’ backup until Mariota returns. The offensive line was an issue going into the season and the quarterback depth, or lack thereof, has quickly become another concern. The Commanders’ season always hinged on Daniels’ health, but that risk is amplified in light of Mariota’s injury.

Can offensive coordinator David Blough develop a game plan that protects Daniels without hindering the offense? And who will Daniels throw to? Wideout Stefon Diggs was ruled out Friday with a hamstring injury, but running back Rachaad White is expected to play. Wide receiver Terry McLaurin’s status is uncertain.

To further complicate matters, heavy rain is expected in the D.C. area on Sunday. Will the forecast impact how the Commanders game-plan for Daniels and the offense?

Quote of the Week

“As an offense, we did not play winning football.” – David Blough on his unit’s performance in Week 4.

Despite Mariota’s injury, the Commanders stuck with the Colts through the first half of Sunday’s game before Indianapolis pulled away. On Sunday, the Commanders are facing a Giants team that has managed to do what they haven’t: Find ways to win games despite injury issues. Blough’s unit will need to level up Sunday to help deliver a win.
entries.author: Michael Errigo

entries.title: Expect to See More Political Ads for Candidates You Can’t Vote For
entries.summary: Media buying experts anticipate there will be more nationwide ad campaigns for Senate candidates in Texas — and maybe Ohio and Michigan.
entries.content:
While Americans sink into their couches this weekend watching football, they may get an unexpected visitor: advertisements for candidates they can’t vote for, running in states hundreds of miles away.

It’s the expected continuation of a phenomenon that began last week when Texas PAC, a group backing Republican Ken Paxton in Texas’ U.S. Senate race, aired a series of ads during FOX’s afternoon football slate, according to AdImpact.

While Dallas Cowboys and Houston Texans fans saw the ad, so, too, did Vikings fans in Minnesota and Jets fans in New York. The reason: It likely cost Texas PAC less money.

“It certainly took a lot of people in the space kind of aback,” said Gerrit Mora, owner of media buying agency Tuesday Digital. “Generally speaking, you really don’t recommend or see that happen very often, or really ever at all.”

This election season, it may only be the beginning with Election Day less than a month away.

“Frankly, I would be surprised if we wouldn’t see another instance of this happening, and I wouldn’t be surprised if we might even see some sort of copycat activity in other races in different spaces as well,” Mora added.

Michael Franz — co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks political advertising — said that in some cases, buying a national advertisement spot can be cheaper than buying a local ad in each of a state’s media markets.

Texas, for instance, has 20 media markets, including two of the country’s biggest: Dallas-Fort Worth and Houston.

Susan Tubbs, owner of the Texas-based media buying and resources company IHN Media Services, said she’s seen that math work out for a client before. They wanted to buy space in 30 different markets, costing $300,000 a week, Tubbs said.

“I’m like, you are wasting your money when we could place $300,000 for the whole month and get the whole country,” she said. “It just didn’t make sense.”

There’s also only so much advertising space on television, Mora said.

PACs, unlike federal candidates’ own campaign committees, don’t get the preferential treatment of a guaranteed “lowest unit cost” and “reasonable access” to ad spots, as required by federal law.

“Those [local spots] get filled up very, very, very quickly,” Mora said. “A PAC is much more at the whim of the overall station dynamics.”

Local news stations are also even more crunched for ad space during events such as NFL games, when there’s more space allocated to national advertisers, Franz said.

That squeeze as Election Day approaches “really does play into” why a PAC would choose to buy a national ad, Mora said.

An advertisement spot during a Cowboys game is also significantly more expensive now than it was at this point of the 2024 election, at least in Dallas.

KDFW-TV, the city’s Fox affiliate, charged a conservative super PAC $200,000 for 30 seconds of airtime as the Cowboys fell to the Baltimore Ravens two years ago, according to records in the Federal Communications Commission’s political ad file database.

This year, Texas PAC paid the station $400,000 for the same amount of late-September airtime, the database shows.

Texas PAC is dropping another $30 million on television ads to support Paxton’s Senate run, Punchbowl News reported Friday.

Mora said the increased rate would affect his decision-making as an ad buyer but that the economics of buying a national political spot are secondary to another consideration: If a national ad draws donors across the country and generates additional buzz in an already-saturated market, it could provide an “edge” for the candidate being supported, he said.

“When you look at those dynamics, and you try to say, ‘OK, where do we spend some money to make a splash?’ I think that ultimately becomes the goal versus strategically placing impressions to drive votes in a certain way,” he said.

“For organizations that just aren’t cost sensitive, doing something like this, it just makes you feel bigger than life sometimes,” Mora added.

Franz also said he “wouldn’t be surprised” by more nationwide ads for statewide races running before Election Day on Nov. 3, although he doesn’t expect to see “a lot of it” between now and then.

Ohio, which similarly has competitive Senate and gubernatorial races, could be a prime candidate for political committees running national ads, Franz said.

Both Franz and Mora also pointed to Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are battling for one of the most competitive Senate seats this cycle.

While speaking to colleagues about pro-Paxton ads filling the national airwaves, Mora said people were surprised by the attention the advertisement earned and the interest it generated.

“I just think that we will see much more of this happening,” he said. “The dollar amounts never cease; just keep getting bigger and bigger and bigger. The media landscape continues to be fragmented. You know, the question of where to place and why is always there.”

entries.title: Federal Judge Blocks DOJ From Accessing State Voter Rolls
entries.summary: The ruling overrides the dozens of DOJ lawsuits meant to force states to turn over their logs in hope of rooting out noncitizen voters.
entries.content:
A federal judge has blocked the Justice Department from accessing state voter rolls to find noncitizen voters and bar them from casting ballots.

Shortly after President Donald Trump authorized the attorney general to contact states for information on suspected election law violations in March 2025, the DOJ began requesting complete and unredacted copies of states’ computerized voter registration lists. The department has filed dozens of lawsuits in attempts to compel enforcement — all of which have been blocked or dismissed by other district courts so far, with a handful of decisions outstanding.

In a decision late Friday, U.S. District Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan said the department was violating several federal laws that govern how agencies collect and control personal data, writing that the policy “flies in the face of duly enacted laws designed to protect Americans.”

The department sought information to find people who could have unlawfully cast a ballot, a sweep of information that includes voters’ full names, dates of birth, residential addresses, driver’s license numbers or partial Social Security numbers.

The DOJ contacted 49 states and D.C., asking state officials to agree to “clean” their logs within 45 days. At least 18 states turned over their rolls, providing information that the DOJ then shared with the Department of Homeland Security to verify voters’ immigration and citizenship status — assuring states that the data would be treated in compliance with the federal Privacy Act.

Sooknanan’s ruling means noncooperative states that sued the government after the directive, as well as the 18 that did comply, no longer have to share their data with federal agencies. DHS and the DOJ can no longer use federal databases to cross-reference rolls they already obtained from the compliant states.

“The challenged policy represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote. But Congress has left that authority where our Constitution has always placed it: with the states,” Sooknanan, a Biden appointee, wrote.

The judge’s decision doesn’t bar the federal government from taking lawful steps to support states’ efforts to maintain accurate voter rolls, nor does it prevent states from maintaining their own voter rolls.

The federal government is expected to seek a stay pending a wider appeal. The DOJ told The Washington Sun it was reviewing the ruling.

The Supreme Court in September cleared the way for states to use the federal government’s overhauled immigration database to purge noncitizens on their own before the midterms, siding with DHS in an unsigned decision after Sooknanan had ordered the system shut down in June. That modified database contained information, including Social Security numbers, in what Sooknanan ruled was also a violation of privacy laws.

The September ruling could come up in a future government appeal of Friday’s ruling.

entries.title: NPS Could Remove Over 500 Trees for Trump’s Planned Golf Course Renovation
entries.summary: A total of 169 trees will be removed starting Saturday, with another 90 trees slated for removal later, the agency said.
entries.content:
By Matthew Daly

WASHINGTON (AP) — The National Park Service has begun a new round of tree-cutting at a historic golf course near the National Mall as the Trump administration proceeds with a plan to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level course.

More than 500 trees “that do not contribute to the historic landscape will be removed” as part of the rehabilitation project, the National Park Service said in a court filing Friday. “No healthy trees that are contributing features of the historical golf course” — including historic cherry trees — will be removed as part of the project, the park service said.

A total of 169 trees will be removed starting Saturday, with another 90 trees slated for removal later, the agency said.

The tree removals come as President Donald Trump has moved to turn the course into a world-class golf venue — part of his grand vision for Washington, D.C., where he has torn down storied structures, remade or renamed others and deployed the National Guard for more than a year.

Some residents fear the planned changes to the golf course — where Trump has visited with a cabinet member, a well-known golf course architect and blueprints — risk altering the character of a place that has served Washingtonians of all income levels for more than a century. Turning the park into an upscale golf course will mean costlier fees and a likely loss of public space.

"The National Park Service is finally implementing a 7-year-old plan to address tree overgrowth at East Potomac Golf Course,'' the Interior Department said in a statement Saturday. The department oversees the park service and other agencies that manage federal lands.

The renovation work will include selective tree and vegetation work to restore the course, the Interior Department said, adding that the work is intended to “help restore the course’s historic character and reopen views toward landmarks, including the Washington Monument, National War College, Potomac River and Washington Channel."

The park service “recognizes the importance of trees to the park and its visitors. This carefully planned work is part of our required stewardship of the park,” the statement said.

The golf course will remain open to the public throughout the renovation effort, although individual holes may temporarily close while work is underway, the agency said.

The 106-year-old public course has been embroiled in a lawsuit since February. Plaintiffs including the DC Preservation League say the Trump administration’s reconstruction would violate the congressional act that created the park in 1897. The group sought an emergency stop-work order this spring because of concerns that work was expected to begin immediately on the course.

Trump, an avid golfer, has posted about the course on social media, “When completed, this Course will have the ability to host Major Golf Tournaments, including The U.S. Open, The Ryder Cup, The PGA Championship, and other top PGA Tour events,” he wrote in late June.

It’s unclear when the course could host any major tournaments, as locations are chosen several years ahead of the events.

entries.title: Trump Blames Zelenskyy for High American Diesel Prices
entries.summary: The president struck a deal with Russia on Friday to bring down American fuel costs, which Zelenskyy said blindsided him.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump urged Ukrainian citizens to replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy, saying he has not done enough to “make a deal” to end the war with Russia and bring down diesel prices.

The president blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries as a contributing factor to increasing diesel prices, telling reporters outside the White House on Saturday: “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”

Fuel costs have widely gone up in association with the U.S.’s war in Iran, which has prompted Iranian attacks on refineries in the Persian Gulf and restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key transportation waterway.

Trump on Friday announced a deal to buy Russian diesel to ease U.S. fuel prices before the midterms, prompting harsh criticism from Zelenskyy. A day later, Russia began a series of strikes that hit Kyiv as well as the country’s Zaporizhzhia region.

Zelenskyy told Axios on Friday that he was blindsided by the deal, later saying it signaled to Russia that it was “apparently permissible” to keep attacking Ukraine.

“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” Zelenskyy wrote on X on Friday. “Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy.”

Trump, who has had a volatile relationship with Zelenskyy, said the Ukrainian leader “chooses not to” end the war, adding that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” targeting refineries. Russia supplies a large portion of the world’s diesel supply, which Trump said has been negatively affected by the strikes.

“He wants to make problems for the world; he wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel,” Trump said Saturday.
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: D.C. Official Who Worked With Formerly Incarcerated Residents Dies in Scooter Crash
entries.summary: Talib Shakir, who once served time in prison, worked with the D.C. government to help those like him.
entries.content:
Talib Shakir, who led a city office that worked with formerly incarcerated residents transitioning to life after prison, was killed in a scooter crash on Capitol Hill Friday night.

Shakir was 50.

“Through his work in public service, most recently leading the Mayor’s Office of Returning Citizen Affairs, Talib was committed to creating opportunities for D.C. residents,” Mayor Muriel Bowser’s office wrote in a statement Saturday afternoon. “We are so grateful for the energy and love he poured into doing just that for the city where he was born, raised, and served.”

According to the Metropolitan Police Department, Shakir was riding an electric scooter Friday night when he collided with another scooter rider at the intersection of 8th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue SE in Eastern Market. Shakir was unconscious and not breathing after the crash and was pronounced dead at a local hospital. The other victim, a woman, was released from the hospital.

Shakir served 25 years in federal prison after being convicted of murder in D.C. in 1993, returning to the city in February 2019. Before assuming leadership of the government office that coordinates efforts to reintegrate former prisoners into civilian life in D.C., Shakir served as deputy director of community relations for the Mayor’s Office of Community Relations and Services.

Shakir recently published a book about his experience, titled “From Cell Block to City Hall: How Lived Experience Becomes the Most Powerful Policy Tool in America.”

“Talib made the most of his second chance and dedicated himself to helping others do the same,” Bowser’s office wrote Saturday. “He loved to mentor young people and prove to them that their city believes in them.”

Each year, anywhere from 2,000 to 2,500 offenders return to D.C. after completing prison sentences, according to the D.C. Criminal Justice Coordinating Council, and roughly two-thirds commit crime again. City officials say inadequate job opportunities and low housing availability are among the most pressing challenges returning citizens face.

“I am heartbroken,” Tomás Talamante, Bowser’s chief of staff, wrote on social media. “Talib was truly one of the kindest, selfless people I have ever met. I am so thankful our paths crossed.”

As of Oct. 10, 33 people have died in traffic crashes on D.C. roads this year — higher than the 17 from the same time period in 2025 but on par with the average over the last three years. The district has seen a recent spate of crashes and fatalities involving electric bikes and scooters, though, including two deaths in September — one of which resulted from a crash between two cyclists.

Electric scooters — including the rentable Lime scooters that are popular in D.C. — have also drawn recent criticism over people using them as getaway vehicles after crimes, or teens crowding sidewalks while riding them in the city.
entries.author: Martin Austermuhle
